SHARED TRIANGULAR SIDES IN PSEUDOLINE ARRANGEMENTS
WILL HOWE, GRANT HUFFMAN, JENSEN KOHLMEYER, AND LIAM KRUER
Abstract.Letdbe the number of edges incident to two bounded triangular faces in a finite affine
arrangement of pseudolines, with each pair crossing exactly once and with only double and triple
crossings. Ift 3 is the number of triple crossings, we proved≤3t 3, answering the compensation
question of Parpalak and Utkin. The proof distributes charge along the normalized boundary of
the union of triangular faces. A double crossing incident to four triangles is treated by restricting
the arrangement to the four pseudolines supporting their opposite sides. This restriction provides
two boundary edges whose unused endpoint charges pay for the crossing.
1.Introduction
An affine pseudoline arrangement is a finite family of proper embedded copies ofRin the plane,
any two meeting exactly once and crossing at their intersection. At a multiple crossing the par-
ticipating pseudolines have the local order of distinct straight lines. Throughout the paper, every
crossing has multiplicity two or three.
Anedgeis a segment of a pseudoline between consecutive crossings. Atriangleis a bounded face
with exactly three edges. In particular, triangles containing further portions of the arrangement
are not counted. An edge issharedif both incident faces are triangles, and it is aboundary edge
if exactly one incident face is a triangle. Writedfor the number of shared edges andt3 for the
number of triple crossings.
Parpalak and Utkin [1, §5.2, (5.5)] ask whetherd≤3t3. Their discharging argument proves the
weaker estimated≤ 92 t3. We establish the proposed inequality.

4.The normalized triangular boundary
Glue the closures of all triangular faces along their shared edges. At any original crossing where
different maximal consecutive fans of triangular sectors meet only at that crossing, separate the
fans. This produces a finite union of compact surfaces with boundary. Holes are permitted and
will not affect the argument.
Aboundary occurrenceof a crossing is a maximal fan ofi≥1consecutive triangular sectors. It
has two incident boundary edges andi−1incident shared edges within the fan. An original crossing
can give several boundary occurrences; these are always kept distinct. At a double boundary
occurrence,i≤3. An interior crossing has all its incident sectors triangular: four at a double
crossing and six at a triple crossing.

The shared edges within such a fan have total endpoint costi−1. After paying this cost, exactly
two units remain. Orient each normalized boundary circuit, and associate both remaining units
with the outgoing boundary edge at the occurrence. Every boundary edge has a unique initial
occurrence, so these edge charges are kept distinct.
A double boundary occurrence has costi−1. For each run of double occurrences between
successive triple occurrences, letD= ∑(i−1). Lemma 4.1 givesD≤2. Pay this cost from the
two units on the boundary edge entering the run from its preceding triple occurrence. Different
runs use different entering edges. Circuits containing only double occurrences have zero cost.
All shared-edge costs at boundary occurrences have now been paid. Moreover, the two units
on a boundary edge joining two triple occurrences remain unused: such an edge does not enter a
nonempty run of double occurrences.
It remains to pay the interior double crossings. Each is incident to four triangles and has cost
four. By Lemma 3.1, choose two outer boundary edges of its four-triangle configuration. Both
endpoints of each chosen edge are triple. The two units on each edge are still available, so the two
edges together pay the cost of the interior double crossing.
These final transfers do not overlap. A boundary edge has exactly one incident triangular face.
If it is an outer edge for an interior double crossingS, the third vertex of that face isS. Thus the
same boundary edge cannot be selected for a different interior double crossing. Charges on different
boundary edges are distinct, even when some of their original vertices coincide.
Every endpoint cost has therefore been paid, and no triple crossing has supplied more than six
units by (5.1). Consequently
